name: Haughton Crater
what_was_tested: Rovers, suits, drilling and crew operations
summary: A 23 km crater in cold polar desert with permafrost and impact rock, used for two decades to rehearse Mars operations. It is far colder and wetter than Mars on average and has an Earth atmosphere.

name: Flashline Mars Arctic Research Station
image_credit: Nsbrihq, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons
what_was_tested: Crew living and working in a habitat and field suits
summary: A simulated Mars base on the rim of Haughton Crater where crews live in a habitat and make field trips in suits. It exercises operations well but cannot reproduce low pressure, gravity or dust.

name: Axel Heiberg perennial springs
image_credit: SaltedSturgeon, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons
what_was_tested: Life in cold salty spring water under permafrost
summary: Salty springs that flow all year through thick permafrost, an analog for possible brine seeps on Mars. They are fed by an Earth water cycle and the surrounding ground is far wetter than Mars.

name: McMurdo Dry Valleys
image_credit: Meile, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
what_was_tested: Viking-era soil tests, ground ice, extremophile survival
summary: The coldest and driest large ice-free area on Earth, used since the 1970s as a Mars soil and ground-ice analog. It is far from people, expensive to reach and already heavily studied.

name: Mount Erebus
image_credit: Richard Waitt, U.S. Geological Survey, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
environment: Active polar volcano with fumarolic ice caves
what_was_tested: Heat-driven ice caves and microbes in volcanic ground
summary: An active polar volcano whose steam vents carve ice caves with microbial life. It points to places on Mars where heat and ice may once have met, though it is far more active than anything Mars now offers.

name: Lake Untersee
image_credit: Wilfried Bauer, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons
what_was_tested: Methane-rich, oxygen-rich ice-covered lake life
summary: A permanently ice-covered lake with very high oxygen and unusual chemistry, used as a model for ice-covered Martian lakes. It is a liquid lake, which present-day Mars does not have.

name: Svalbard (Bockfjorden volcanic complex)
what_was_tested: Rover instrument and biosignature testing at volcanic springs
summary: Arctic volcanic cones and mineral springs used by the Arctic Mars Analog Svalbard Expedition to test instruments in Mars-like carbonate rocks. It is wetter, greener and gentler than Mars.

name: Pavilion Lake
image_credit: Murray Foubister, CC BY-SA 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons
what_was_tested: Underwater exploration and sampling by crews and robots
summary: A lake with living microbial rock formations where divers and submersibles rehearsed exploring from a distance with delay. It is an environment Mars does not have today.

name: Kilbourne Hole
image_credit: Dicklyon, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons
what_was_tested: Planetary geology training and rover tests in a dry crater
summary: A dry volcanic crater with fresh basalt and exposed mantle rocks, used to train astronauts in geology. It is warm, thinly vegetated and very handy, but Earth gravity and atmosphere still apply.

name: Potrillo volcanic field
image_credit: NASA Earth Observatory images by Jesse Allen, using Landsat data from the U.S. G, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
what_was_tested: Basalt field terrain tests
summary: A basalt field with cones, lava flows and maars close to Kilbourne Hole. It matches lunar mare-style basalt ground in texture, not in vacuum or radiation.

name: SP Crater
image_credit: USGS, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
environment: Cinder cone and blocky lava flow
what_was_tested: Astronaut geology training and rover mobility on rugged flows
summary: A young cinder cone and rough lava flow that Apollo crews and later rover teams used as a stand-in for the Moon. The ground is rocky and fine dust is abundant, but the air is thick.

name: Cinder Lake crater field
what_was_tested: Landing and crew training among explosive craters
summary: A field of blast craters made in 1967 so Apollo crews could practise driving and landing among craters. It is a purpose-built stage rather than a natural match.

name: Merriam Crater
what_was_tested: Source of JSC-1A lunar regolith simulant
summary: A volcanic cinder cone whose ash was crushed to make JSC-1A, the long-standing lunar regolith simulant. Good for testing machines on dust, not for chemistry of real lunar soil.

name: Black Point lava flow
what_was_tested: Rover navigation across rough basalt
summary: A fresh basalt flow used for rover and crew mobility trials. Rough lava ground matches parts of lunar and Martian terrain.

name: Meteor Crater
image_credit: National Map Seamless Server, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
what_was_tested: Crater geology training
summary: A 1.2 km, 50,000-year-old simple impact crater, the textbook for how craters form. It is one of the best-known Earth craters and well studied.

name: Craters of the Moon
wikipedia_title: Craters of the Moon National Monument and Preserve
image_credit: BroMcjoe, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons
environment: Basalt lava field with lava tubes
what_was_tested: Astronaut training, science-operations rehearsals, lava-tube access
summary: A huge young basalt field with tubes, cones and rift cracks used since Apollo. It has frozen caves and rough flows like those suspected on the Moon and Mars, with a cold, dry climate and Earth air.

name: Lava Beds National Monument
image_credit: U.S. National Park Service, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
what_was_tested: Rover cave exploration
summary: Hundreds of lava tubes in cold, dry high desert, used to rehearse robots going underground. A good cave match, but gravity and air still differ.

name: Lunar Crater volcanic field
image_credit: TheAustinMan, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons
what_was_tested: Geology training and instrument tests
summary: A basalt field named for its look, with cones and a large maar. Hot dry desert terrain with Earth air.

name: Mauna Kea (Puʻu Nene)
image_credit: Vadim Kurland, CC BY 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons
what_was_tested: JSC Mars-1 simulant and cinder-cone mobility
summary: A high, cold, dry volcano with weathered ash used to make JSC Mars-1 soil simulant. The weather and plants are very different from Mars.

name: Mauna Loa (HI-SEAS)
image_credit: J.D. Griggs, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
what_was_tested: Crew isolation and long-duration habitat studies
summary: A habitat on a barren basalt slope where crews live in isolation for months. It tests people more than ground, since the setting is a high-altitude basalt desert on an island.

name: Kīlauea and Kaʻū Desert
what_was_tested: Astronaut training and lava-flow observation
summary: A very active basaltic volcano with fresh lava and tubes, and a dry desert side with weathered ash. It shows basalt processes in action, with far more water and life than Mars.

name: Saddleback Basalt (Mojave)
image_credit: Daniel Mayer (mav), CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons
what_was_tested: Source of Mojave Mars Simulant
summary: A basalt quarry in the Mojave Desert that supplies the Mojave Mars Simulant. Useful for testing equipment on dusty rock, not for the real chemistry of Mars.

name: Zzyzx
image_credit: Stammberger1973, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons
what_was_tested: Desert and playa studies
summary: A dry lake and desert research station with mineral springs. It is a hot desert with wind-blown dust, but humid pockets and hot summers set it apart from Mars.

name: Death Valley
image_credit: NASA, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
environment: Hot hyperarid basin with fans and salts
what_was_tested: Alluvial fan, salt pan and dust studies
summary: A hot, dry basin with salt flats and fans that is a classic landform analog for Mars. It is far hotter than Mars.

name: White Sands gypsum dunes
image_credit: uncredited National Park Service employee, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
what_was_tested: Dune processes and gypsum minerals
summary: A huge field of gypsum dunes like gypsum-rich dunes seen near Mars's north pole. Gypsum dunes are rare on Earth.

name: Mars Desert Research Station
image_credit: The Mars Society / MDRS, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons
what_was_tested: Crew operations in a simulated Mars base
summary: A desert habitat in red Jurassic rock where crews rehearse life and work on Mars. It has a human feel of Mars missions, not Mars conditions.

name: San Rafael Swell
image_credit: AustinAdesso, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons
what_was_tested: Layered sedimentary geology and canyons
summary: A desert uplift with layered rock, canyons and mesas similar to eroded Martian layers. Mild weather and sparse plants.

name: Bonneville Salt Flats
image_credit: Asibasm, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons
what_was_tested: Rover driving on very flat salt
summary: A flat salt pan useful for rover driving tests and evaporite studies. Its flatness is unusual even on Mars.

name: Stillwater Complex
image_credit: Russell Lee, Office of War Information photographer, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
what_was_tested: Source of NU-LHT lunar highland simulant
summary: A layered igneous intrusion with anorthosite used for lunar highland simulant. Its rock matches the Moon's bright crust but the mountain climate does not.

name: Duluth Complex
image_credit: Wikimedia Commons contributor, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
what_was_tested: Source of MLS-1 lunar mare simulant
summary: A large body of gabbro and anorthosite that supplied MLS-1 lunar mare simulant. Cold and forested at the surface.

name: Sudbury Basin
image_credit: User:Vesta, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
what_was_tested: Impact melt and shatter-cone studies
summary: A 130 km, two-billion-year-old impact structure with a thick melt sheet and shatter cones. A deep, eroded crater unlike fresh lunar craters.

name: Mistastin Lake
image_credit: NASA/USGS, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
what_was_tested: Rover and sampling tests in lunar-like rock
summary: A 28 km crater cut into anorthosite, the rock of the lunar highlands, used for CSA lunar analog missions. Arctic coastal conditions.

name: Shawmere Anorthosite
what_was_tested: Lunar highland rock matches
summary: An anorthosite body of the same rock type as the lunar highlands. The setting is forest and small lakes.

name: Askja
image_credit: Michael Ryan, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
what_was_tested: Apollo geology training, rover and drilling tests
summary: A highland caldera with lava, pumice and a lake where Apollo crews trained. It is cold, rough and bare, but wetter than the Moon.

name: Holuhraun
image_credit: Wikimedia Commons contributor, see Commons, via Wikimedia Commons
what_was_tested: Fresh lava flow morphology
summary: A basalt lava field made in 2014-15, fresh and well mapped. It is like large lunar and Martian lava plains in shape.

name: Lambahraun
what_was_tested: Lava tube exploration
summary: A lava field in the Icelandic highlands with caves. A cold, cave-rich basalt site.

name: Ries crater
what_was_tested: Impact breccia studies and crew training
summary: A 24 km crater 15 million years old, used to train Apollo 14 crews in impact deposits. Eroded and farmland-covered.

name: Bletterbach
image_credit: Wikimedia Commons contributor, see Commons, via Wikimedia Commons
what_was_tested: Layered rock mapping
summary: A canyon in alpine layered rock. Used to teach layered geology in a compact setting.

name: Timanfaya
image_credit: MiljenkoSuljic, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons
what_was_tested: Rover and astronaut field tests
summary: A harsh volcanic field of basalt that ESA uses for astronaut and rover geology training. Warm dry island setting with a thin soil of lava ash.

name: Corona lava tube (Cueva de los Verdes)
image_credit: Wikimedia Commons contributor, see Commons, via Wikimedia Commons
what_was_tested: Cave exploration and robotics
summary: A kilometre-long lava tube used by ESA to train explorers and test robots underground. Its entrance and air differ from a lunar tube.

name: Teide
image_credit: Thomas Wolf, www.foto-tw.de, CC BY-SA 3.0 de, via Wikimedia Commons
what_was_tested: Dry volcanic terrain tests
summary: A high dry volcano with a flat caldera floor of ash and pumice. It is a sunny, cold, high-altitude volcanic desert.

name: Mount Etna
image_credit: BenAveling, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons
what_was_tested: Robotic geology on active volcano ground
summary: A very active volcano used for ESA robot-and-scientist field campaigns. Lava ground and ash, with vegetation lower down.

name: Vulcano
image_credit: No machine-readable author provided. NormanEinstein assumed (based on copyright , CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons
what_was_tested: Hot acid vents and sulfur minerals
summary: A volcanic island with strong hot vents and sulfur, like some Martian hydrothermal deposits.

name: Río Tinto
what_was_tested: Drilling for subsurface life with the MARTE rover
summary: A river made red and acidic by iron and sulfur minerals, with jarosite like that found by Opportunity on Mars. It carries lots of water and is shaped by mining.

name: Tabernas Desert
image_credit: Dgalan, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons
what_was_tested: Rover tests in dry badlands
summary: Europe's only true desert, with badlands and gypsum, used in rover field trials. It is mild and has plants.

name: Lofoten anorthosites
image_credit: Lukas Beck, CC BY 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons
what_was_tested: Lunar highland rock source
summary: An island chain with anorthosite mountains like the Moon's highlands. Cool, wet Atlantic climate.

name: Naajat anorthosite
what_was_tested: Lunar highland simulant source
summary: A Greenland body of old anorthosite similar to lunar highland rock. Remote and cold, with frequent snow.

name: Boulby mine
image_credit: Dave Eagle, CC BY-SA 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons
environment: Deep underground salt and potash mine
what_was_tested: Robotic life-detection and underground rover tests
summary: A working mine 1.1 km down in Permian salt, used for the MINAR Mars analog campaigns. A rare deep underground analog setting.

name: Dhofar (AMADEE-18)
image_credit: NordNordWest, CC BY-SA 3.0 de, via Wikimedia Commons
what_was_tested: Mars habitat simulation in a desert
summary: A hot desert site chosen for the AMADEE-18 Mars mission simulation. It was chosen for terrain, dryness and access.

name: Makhtesh Ramon
image_credit: Hagai Agmon-Snir حچاي اچمون-سنير חגי אגמון-שניר, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons
what_was_tested: Mars simulation and rover tests
summary: A 40 km erosion crater with layered rock in the Negev desert. It looks like a Martian canyon but is mild and sunny.

name: Armash
what_was_tested: Mars simulation in Armenia
summary: A volcanic highland site used for the AMADEE-24 Mars simulation. It is a recent, less common choice.

name: Erfoud region
image_credit: Holger Uwe Schmitt, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons
what_was_tested: ExoMars rover trials
summary: A Saharan desert near Erfoud used to field test the ExoMars rover and Mars crew work. A hot, dry dust setting.

name: Danakil Depression
image_credit: Val Rime, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons
environment: Hot acid springs and salt plain
what_was_tested: Life limits in hot acidic brine
summary: One of the hottest places on Earth with acid springs and salt flats at the edge of life. A strong extremophile analog and far from Mars on temperature.

name: Namib Desert (Gobabeb)
image_credit: Jeff Schmaltz, MODIS Land Rapid Response Team, NASA GSFC, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
what_was_tested: Dune studies and desert research
summary: The oldest desert on Earth with giant dunes. Sea fog gives it a moisture that Mars lacks.

name: Yungay (Atacama)
image_credit: NASA, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
what_was_tested: Instrument tests in the driest soil on Earth
summary: One of the driest places on Earth with oxidising soils like Mars. It is much warmer than Mars on average.

name: Salar Grande
what_was_tested: Life in salt rock
summary: A huge salt pan in the Atacama where microbes live inside salt crusts. A good salt-biosignature analog.

name: Salar de Uyuni
image_credit: Anouchka Unel, FAL, via Wikimedia Commons
what_was_tested: Salt flat geology and rover tests
summary: The world's largest salt flat, extremely flat and bright. Its altitude gives thin air.

name: Ojos del Salado and Laguna Negra
image_credit: sergejf, CC BY-SA 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons
environment: High volcano with a crater lake
what_was_tested: High-altitude life and volcanic lake studies
summary: The highest volcano on Earth with a crater lake and extreme UV. Altitude brings thin air and strong radiation.

name: Pali Aike
image_credit: Janitoalevic, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons
what_was_tested: Basalt field and lava tube studies
summary: A cold windy basalt plain with lava tubes. A less visited analog in the far south.

name: Lonar Crater
image_credit: Aditya Laghate, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons
environment: Impact crater in basalt with salt lake
what_was_tested: Impact in basalt for Mars-like geology
summary: A 1.8 km, 50,000-year-old crater in basalt with a salty alkaline lake. It is one of the few impact craters in basalt, like the Moon and Mars.

name: Tso Kar and Puga
image_credit: GerthMichael, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons
environment: High cold desert with salt lakes and hot springs
what_was_tested: Cold desert and spring research
summary: A high, cold desert with salt lakes and hot springs. Some of the least-visited ground in this list.

name: Qaidam Basin (Lenghu)
image_credit: Croquant, CC BY 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons
what_was_tested: Mars base simulation in a desert
summary: A high, dry basin with yardangs and salt, used for Mars camp training in China. It is among the less written-about Mars analog places.

name: Pilbara
environment: Ancient rock with oldest life traces
what_was_tested: Biosignature preservation in ancient rocks
summary: A hot region with some of the oldest rocks and microbial fossils on Earth. It guides what traces of early life might look like on Mars.

name: Lake Tyrrell
image_credit: Rueparadis, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons
what_was_tested: Gypsum and salt lake studies
summary: A large salt lake whose gypsum is like gypsum found on Mars. A less common analog in Australia.

name: Cuatro Ciénegas
what_was_tested: Ancient microbial ecosystems
summary: A desert valley of springs and ponds with ancient bacteria. It is water-rich, unlike Mars.

name: Yellowstone silica springs
image_credit: Mav at English Wikipedia, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons
what_was_tested: Silica deposits similar to Spirit's finds
summary: Hot-spring silica like that found by the Spirit rover in Gusev. A supply of liquid water and heat is present here.

name: Fox permafrost tunnel
what_was_tested: Ground ice and cold-tunnel work
summary: A tunnel dug into frozen ground that exposes old ice and soil, like ice buried at high Martian latitudes. A rare place to stand inside ground ice.

name: Kamchatka (Mutnovsky)
image_credit: Jerzy Franek (my friend), Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
what_was_tested: Hydrothermal systems and ice caves
summary: A cold volcanic land with hot springs and ice caves. It is remote and rarely used in the usual analog lists.

name: Lut Desert
image_credit: Ninaras, CC BY 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons
what_was_tested: Extreme heat and yardang terrain
summary: Where satellites measure the hottest land surface on Earth, with yardangs and dunes. A less-studied hot desert candidate.
